Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Jeweler
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Offender Cues: Seeing the offender, Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside

Vignette:
Maya sat in the intake office with her hands folded tightly in her lap, a delicate silver ring on her right thumb catching the light. She was fifty years old, a jeweler by trade, and she had not set foot in her own workshop in over three months. She spoke softly at first, then with a kind of hollow precision, as though she had rehearsed the story many times but never said it aloud.

The assault had happened in the back room of her store, just before closing. A man she had seen browsing for nearly twenty minutes had followed her when she went to retrieve a repair from the safe. He was not a stranger in the way she had once understood the word—he had been a customer, polite, unremarkable. But when she turned around, he was there, and everything after that was a series of snapshots that did not connect. She remembered the cold pressure of the floor tiles against her cheek. She remembered the sound of a display case rattling as her shoulder hit it. She remembered nothing of the moments in between, and she had never been able to recall his face fully, though she knew she would recognize him if she saw him. That partial clarity was the most maddening part. Some details were so vivid they burned—the smell of his jacket, the weight of his hand on her wrist—while entire seconds were simply missing, as though her mind had cut them out with scissors.

For the first few weeks afterward, Maya had tried to go back to work. She had told herself that the store was her life, that she had built it over twenty years, that she could not let one man take it. But every time she walked through the front door, she felt a wave of nausea so immediate and so physical that she had to brace herself against the counter. The nausea did not come from memory alone. It came from the smell of the cleaning solution she used on the display cases, from the particular angle of the afternoon light that fell across the back hallway, from the sound of the bell above the door. She began to avoid those things without deciding to. She stopped using the back room entirely. She started locking the front door during business hours, opening it only for customers she recognized. Then she stopped opening it at all.

She had come to believe that her reactions since the attack proved something fundamental about her character. A stronger person, she thought, would have fought back. A stronger person would have screamed. A stronger person would not be sitting here, unable to work, unable to leave her apartment without scanning every room for exits. She felt dirty in a way that no amount of showering could fix. She had scrubbed her hands raw in the weeks after the assault, and still the feeling lingered—a greasy, invisible film that she could not wash away. She had stopped letting people touch her. She had stopped wanting them to.

Her social world had shrunk to almost nothing. A friend had called to tell her about a mutual acquaintance whose husband had died suddenly, and Maya had hung up mid-sentence. She could not bear to hear about loss. It was not that she lacked sympathy; it was that the word itself felt like a door opening onto something she could not contain. She had started to feel dead inside, numb in a way that frightened her more than the fear did. At least fear felt like something. The numbness felt like she had already disappeared.

The only places she felt safe were her apartment and her sister’s house, and even those had begun to feel fragile. She had stopped going to the grocery store. She ordered everything online. When she had to leave for a doctor’s appointment, she scanned the parking lot before getting out of the car, and she sat with her back to a wall the entire time. Strangers approaching her—even a cashier asking if she needed help—sent a spike of alarm through her chest that took hours to settle.

What finally brought Maya to seek help was not the fear or the nausea or the numbness. It was the realization that she had not touched her tools in four months. Her hands, which had spent thirty years shaping gold and silver into things of precision and beauty, now sat idle in her lap. She was afraid that if she did not find a way back, she would never find it at all. And she was afraid, too, that the man who had taken so much from her in those missing seconds would end up taking everything else. She did not know if she could be fixed. She only knew that she could not keep living this way.
